abstract:
Establishing direct peer-to-peer UDP connections across Network Address Translators (NATs) is a common challenge in networked applications, typically requiring complex protocol machinery. This library addresses that problem by providing a simplified implementation of the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) protocol, covering both client-side and server-side roles, written in C with no external dependencies. It targets a single UDP component per session within a standard single-gateway network topology, which covers the majority of real-world use cases including WebRTC Data Channels and multiplexed RTP/RTCP streams.

Technically, the library implements a full ICE agent per RFC 5245 and RFC 8445, incorporating STUN (RFC 5389/8489) for NAT discovery, TURN (RFC 5766/8656) for relay-based traversal, TCP candidates (RFC 6544), ICE consent freshness (RFC 7675), and an SDP-based interface (RFC 8839). It supports IPv4/IPv6 dual-stack operation and optional multiplexing across a single UDP port. A lightweight built-in STUN/TURN server is included and can be disabled at compile time. The sole optional dependency is an external cryptography library for SHA-1 and SHA-256, with internal fallback implementations provided. The library builds via CMake or Make and supports GNU/Linux, Android, FreeBSD, macOS, iOS, and Windows, with bindings available for Rust.

A standard bump allocator's primary limitation is its inability to reclaim memory in arbitrary order, causing allocations to accumulate until a full arena reset. This implementation addresses that constraint with a modified bump allocator that supports incremental deallocation from the top of the allocation stack. The core mechanism appends new allocations sequentially to the end of a contiguous memory region, as in a conventional bump allocator, but tracks free status such that when the most recently allocated block is freed, the allocator also reclaims any immediately preceding blocks already marked free. This coalescing-from-top behavior allows common stack-like allocation patterns — where memory is freed in reverse allocation order — to avoid leaking memory across repeated function calls. The library implements the full standard allocator interface, including `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `free`, `aligned_alloc`, `posix_memalign`, and related functions, and is compiled as a shared library injectable via `LD_PRELOAD` on Linux or `DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES` on macOS without modifying the target program. Underlying memory is obtained via `brk`. Compilation options allow configuring allocation alignment (required to be a power of two), `errno` propagation, and single-threaded mode to eliminate locking overhead. The codebase is written in ANSI C with minimal platform-specific code, making porting straightforward.

This project addresses the challenge of understanding para-virtualized device development by providing a concrete, self-contained educational example of how virtual devices and guest drivers interact in a QEMU/Linux virtualization environment. The target architecture is AArch64, and the demonstration uses a stopwatch as a minimal but complete use case.

The approach involves implementing both sides of the virtualization boundary: a custom virtual device integrated into QEMU (host side) and a corresponding Linux kernel driver in the guest, communicating via three resource types discovered through the Device Tree Blob (DTB). These resources consist of a trapping memory region (used for MMIO-style communication), a pass-through memory region, and an interrupt line. The stopwatch logic executes on the host within QEMU, while the user interface operates in guest userland through sysfs and debugfs virtual files exposed by the kernel module.

The build system automates the entire toolchain: downloading QEMU, Linux, and BusyBox source trees; applying minimal patches to integrate the custom device and driver; compiling a guest kernel and root filesystem; and launching the VM for demonstration. Docker support is included for reproducibility. The repository is structured to separate static source components (device, driver, guest scripts, patches) from generated build artifacts, making the host-guest interface and MMIO mechanism explicit and inspectable for educational purposes.

A macOS application addresses the absence of an "Active Desktop" feature—popularized on older Windows systems—that allows users to display live web content as their desktop wallpaper. Rather than static images, the tool renders any user-specified website directly on the desktop layer, enabling dynamic, interactive, or periodically updating content to serve as the desktop background. Technically, the application is built natively for macOS using Swift, leveraging system-level windowing to position a web rendering layer behind all other windows but above the standard wallpaper. It uses a Swift-based user defaults wrapper for persistent settings storage and integrates a keyboard shortcuts library to allow user-customizable global hotkeys for controlling the application. The approach essentially creates a transparent, always-present browser window anchored to the desktop layer, which loads and continuously displays whatever URL the user configures. This enables use cases such as live dashboards, clock or weather widgets, custom HTML/CSS art, or any other web-based content as a desktop environment. The application is distributed as a closed-source macOS app, developed and maintained by a single author, with issue tracking handled through a public repository for bug reports and feature requests despite the source code itself not being publicly available.

A lightweight unit testing framework addresses the challenge of integrating tests directly into C and C++ source files without requiring separate test harnesses or boilerplate infrastructure. The approach embeds test functions alongside the code under test, with a companion executable discovering and running those tests by inspecting symbol tables in compiled binaries.

Technically, the framework provides two header files targeting different C standards: one for C99 and later using a macro that conditionally compiles test functions only when a preprocessor symbol is defined, and one for ANSI C (C89) using a function-style macro with an explicit return value. Both macros generate static functions whose symbols are later located by the runner executable using the POSIX `nm` utility, which enumerates exported symbols in the compiled binary. The runner invokes each discovered test function, captures its output prefixed with the test name, and reports whether the test succeeded or terminated abnormally (including via signals such as those raised by `assert` failures). The output format is deliberately plain text, designed for downstream processing with standard Unix tools like `awk`, `grep`, and `sed`, with example scripts provided for common filtering tasks such as isolating failures or routing per-test output to individual log files. The system targets POSIX.1-2001 compliant environments and requires symbols to be exported from the compiled artifact, which may necessitate building as a shared library depending on toolchain defaults.

A C library addresses the challenge of building desktop graphical user interfaces in C while leveraging familiar web frontend development paradigms. The approach integrates a built-in CSS engine, a React-inspired component model, and TypeScript/JSX-based tooling to allow developers with web experience to construct native desktop UIs without a browser runtime. Technically, the system is composed of several modular sub-libraries: a graphics layer handling font management, text layout, image processing, and 2D rendering; a CSS parser and selector engine; a platform abstraction layer managing window creation, message loops, timers, and input methods; a core UI library handling component lifecycle, event queues, style computation, and drawing; and a file-system-based router for page navigation. A command-line tool preprocesses TypeScript/JSX configuration files and generates corresponding C source code and resource files, enabling a workflow that mirrors modern web frontend toolchains including support for Tailwind CSS, CSS Modules, and Sass. The library supports Windows and Linux, implements DPI-aware automatic scaling for high-resolution displays, and renders all components through custom drawing to ensure consistent cross-platform appearance. The update described improves the layout engine and rendering pipeline performance within this architecture.

A pure C implementation of the WebRTC protocol stack addresses the challenge of enabling real-time peer-to-peer audio and video communication on resource-constrained embedded and IoT devices where higher-level language runtimes are impractical. The library is written entirely in C to minimize footprint — the compiled library remains under 200 kilobytes — and is designed with cross-compilation as a primary concern, supporting architectures including x64 and ARMv5 on Linux, macOS, and Windows.

The implementation covers the full WebRTC negotiation and media pipeline: STUN/TURN-based NAT traversal, DTLS/SRTP for encrypted media transport, SCTP-based data channels, and RTP/RTCP with support for NACKs, FIR, and PLI congestion-control callbacks. Supported codecs include VP8, H.264, Opus, and G.711 PCM in both A-law and µ-law variants. The library exposes raw media input/output rather than bundling capture or encoding, leaving the media pipeline under developer control. A signaling client is included for session negotiation, and STUN/TURN infrastructure is provided by a managed cloud backend. Dependencies include OpenSSL or mbedTLS for cryptography, libsrtp2 for SRTP, libusrsctp for SCTP, and libwebsockets for the WebSocket signaling transport. The build system uses CMake and can compile all dependencies from source, simplifying cross-compilation workflows for embedded targets.

This resource addresses the challenge of coordinating disparate open-source software efforts and informational materials related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The approach is a community-maintained curated directory that aggregates active technical projects and authoritative data sources in one place, enabling contributors and developers to discover where assistance is needed and avoid duplicating effort.

Technically, the collection organizes several categories of tools: geographic mapping applications for locating testing sites, web-based clinical pre-screening and risk-assessment tools, epidemiological modeling systems that project outbreak trajectories and hospital capacity demand, distributed computing initiatives for protein folding simulation, and data APIs (both REST and GraphQL) that expose aggregated case statistics from institutional data repositories. A dashboard component provides visualization of testing and case metrics. On the informational side, the directory links to genomic surveillance datasets, curated scientific literature databases, and public health authority guidance from global and national bodies.

The compilation also surfaces unmet needs, specifically community-level logistics tools such as coordinated grocery procurement to reduce public exposure for vulnerable populations, and mechanisms for supporting individuals and small businesses facing sudden income loss. Contributions are accepted via a simple append-to-list convention, keeping coordination overhead minimal and allowing rapid community expansion of the directory as new projects emerge.

A command-line utility addresses the common need among systems programmers, storage engineers, and low-level developers for a dedicated calculator that understands data storage units, binary prefixes, and hardware addressing schemes—tasks poorly served by general-purpose calculators. The tool provides both a REPL interface and single-execution mode for evaluating arithmetic expressions involving storage units (e.g., `(2GiB * 2) / (2KiB >> 2)`), performing SI/IEC unit conversions, and computing byte addresses.

Technically, the utility is implemented in C, depending on standard libc and GNU Readline (or BSD Editline) for interactive input with history support. It supports 128-bit integer arithmetic where the compiler provides `__uint128_t`, falling back to 64-bit, and uses `long double` for floating-point operations. Storage-mode expressions accept decimal and hexadecimal operands with SI/IEC prefixes; a separate general-purpose mode adds bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, complement, shifts), transcendental and power functions (exp, log, ln, pow, root), and variadic summation. The tool also handles LBA-to-CHS and CHS-to-LBA conversions with configurable sector size and cylinder/track geometry parameters, base conversion between binary, decimal, and hexadecimal, and bit-position visualization. Input can be provided interactively, piped, or redirected from a file, and the last computed result is stored in a reusable variable within REPL sessions.

This project addresses the challenge of simulating emergent evolutionary behavior in a cellular automaton framework. Rather than using fixed survival rules, the system introduces autonomous agents ("piks") that each carry a genome encoding behavioral responses to environmental stimuli.

Technically, each agent occupies a cell on a 2D grid and maintains a directional state. At each simulation tick, an agent senses the occupancy of its eight neighboring cells, producing a binary configuration equivalent to an 8-bit integer, yielding 256 possible input states. Each agent's genome is a lookup table mapping each of these 256 configurations to one of three actions: move forward into an empty cell, turn left or right, or reproduce. Reproduction consumes the agent in the forward cell as a resource, places an offspring in the rear cell facing the opposite direction, and introduces a small random mutation probability, enabling gradual evolutionary divergence across generations.

The simulator is a command-line tool with optional graphical output, configurable world dimensions, population size, random seed, and frame rate. World states are serializable to and loadable from files, with optional periodic autosaving and a tick-count stop condition. A magic file descriptor allows the host system's file-identification utility to recognize the proprietary world file format. The design intentionally keeps agent mechanics minimal to isolate and observe emergent evolutionary dynamics.

A compiled, performance-oriented programming language addresses the gap between low-level systems languages and higher-level ergonomic languages, targeting real-time applications such as video games and engine development. The language derives its syntax and semantics primarily from C#, while incorporating C-style bare-metal explicitness and drawing ergonomic influences from more modern systems languages. Memory management is entirely manual, with first-class support for custom allocators; the runtime provides leak detection and guaranteed protection against use-after-free and double-deletion errors, all of which can be disabled in release builds for maximum throughput. A distinctive feature allows mixing optimization levels on a per-type or per-method granularity, enabling performance-critical code paths to run at full optimization while the remainder of the codebase retains debuggability. The language is developed alongside an integrated IDE environment that provides autocomplete, code fix suggestions, reformatting, refactoring tools, type inspection, hot code swapping via runtime recompilation, and a built-in profiler. The IDE also includes a general-purpose native debugger capable of debugging applications written in any language, positioned as a standalone alternative to existing platform debuggers for C and C++ developers. The project is open source under an MIT license and targets high-performance real-time application development as its primary design objective.

A bioinformatics library addresses the problem of identifying sequence similarities in biological sequences, particularly RNA viruses, by providing efficient implementations of classical pairwise sequence alignment algorithms. The core challenge is aligning two sequences—DNA, RNA, or protein strings—to reveal regions of similarity that may reflect evolutionary, structural, or functional relationships. The library implements four well-established dynamic programming algorithms: Needleman-Wunsch for global alignment, Hirschberg's algorithm (a space-efficient variant of global alignment), Smith-Waterman for local alignment, and Gotoh's algorithm in both local and global forms, the latter introducing affine gap penalties to better model biological insertion and deletion events. Technically, the library is implemented in C++ using a templated design, allowing alignment over arbitrary sequence and character types with a configurable gap character. Users instantiate a typed aligner object parameterized with a scoring system that specifies match rewards and gap penalties, then call an alignment method on two input strings to retrieve an annotated alignment result. The scoring system is configurable at construction time, enabling tuning for different biological contexts. The interface is minimal, requiring only standard C++ strings as input, and returns structured alignment objects representing the gapped sequences and their correspondence.

A persistent storage library for React Native addresses the limitations of existing mobile storage solutions by providing multi-type data support, multiple isolated database instances, and optional encryption within a single lightweight package. The approach wraps an established memory-mapped key-value storage engine (originally developed for a large-scale messaging application) through a C++ layer exposed to JavaScript via the React Native JSI (JavaScript Interface) bridge, bypassing the asynchronous serialization overhead of the traditional bridge architecture.

Technically, the underlying engine uses memory-mapped files (mmap) to keep in-memory state synchronized with on-disk data, and employs Protocol Buffers for value encoding and decoding, yielding sub-millisecond read/write operations. The JSI binding allows synchronous calls directly from JavaScript without thread-hopping. The library exposes a loader-style API for constructing named database instances with optional AES CFB-128 encryption backed by platform keystores (iOS Keychain, Android Keystore). React hooks (`useMMKVStorage` and `useIndex`) provide reactive, persisted state that automatically propagates storage changes to UI components. A Transaction Manager system allows lifecycle callbacks (before/after read, write, delete) to be registered per key pattern, enabling custom secondary indexes to be maintained incrementally. Multi-process access is supported for use cases such as app extensions and home screen widgets. The library also includes compatibility adapters for redux-persist and supports the Expo bare workflow.

This project addresses the gap in accessible learning resources for developers who want to use the PyTorch C++ frontend (LibTorch) rather than the Python API. While Python-based deep learning tutorials are abundant, equivalent C++ implementations covering a structured progression from fundamentals to advanced techniques are scarce. The approach taken is to provide a comprehensive, structured collection of C++ tutorial implementations spanning beginner through advanced topics, organized into thematic categories. The basics tier covers tensor operations, linear regression, logistic regression, and feedforward neural networks. The intermediate tier includes convolutional networks, deep residual networks, recurrent and bidirectional recurrent networks, and a language model. The advanced tier addresses generative adversarial networks, variational autoencoders, neural style transfer, and image captioning using a CNN-attention-RNN architecture. Technically, each tutorial is implemented in C++17 using the LibTorch API and built via CMake, which also handles optional automated dataset downloading and TorchScript module generation. The build system supports selective compilation by category or individual tutorial, and accommodates CPU and multiple CUDA versions across Linux, macOS, and Windows platforms. Interactive Jupyter-style notebooks are also available via the xeus-cling kernel, and containerized deployment is supported through Docker with volume mounting for dependency caching.

This template addresses the setup friction involved in combining the ncurses terminal UI library with the Bazel build system for C++ projects. Developers building text-based user interfaces in C++ must typically configure build tooling manually, reconcile dependency management between system-installed libraries and build rules, and establish project scaffolding from scratch. The proposed approach provides a ready-to-use starter repository that wires together these components so development can begin immediately without build configuration overhead.

Technically, the template integrates the ncurses library — which provides terminal-independent APIs for constructing GUI-like text interfaces, optimizing screen redraws, and reducing latency in remote shell environments — into a Bazel-managed C++ build graph. The repository includes Bazel build files defining targets for both a runnable binary (demonstrating scrolling text output) and a unit test suite. Platform-specific instructions cover library installation via package managers on Debian/Ubuntu Linux and macOS, with separate configuration files provided for Ubuntu compatibility. The project is also structured for use within Visual Studio Code. An included API quick-reference document supplements the starter code by summarizing common ncurses function signatures. Overall, the template targets C++ developers who want to build terminal applications using a hermetic, reproducible build system without manually authoring the underlying build and dependency configuration.

This project addresses the challenge of creating an accessible, gesture-based musical instrument using low-cost microcontroller hardware. The proposed approach maps physical proximity to discrete musical notes, allowing a performer to play melodies by moving their hand or body toward or away from an ultrasonic distance sensor.

Technically, the system runs on a microcontroller paired with an ultrasonic ranger and a small speaker module. The ranger continuously measures distance within a configurable working range (defined by near and far threshold constants in centimeters). This range is divided into equal subranges, with each subrange corresponding to one note in a predefined melody array. Notes are stored as frequency values indexed by position, following a standard octave-and-note naming convention. When an object is detected within the working range, the system calculates which subrange the current distance falls into and retrieves the corresponding note index, using integer division without rounding. The indexed note is then played through one of two selectable output methods: a built-in hardware tone function, or a manually generated waveform via digital output toggling with delays. Direction of traversal is configurable, allowing melodies to play either as the performer approaches or retreats from the sensor. Pin assignments and range parameters are set via preprocessor directives, making the system straightforward to adapt for different hardware configurations. The project is intended primarily for educational exploration of sensor-driven audio generation.

A full-text search engine written in C++ addresses the need for a high-performance, research-oriented platform for experimenting with information retrieval (IR) techniques at large scale. The system targets scalability and efficiency research rather than general-purpose deployment, providing a controlled environment for evaluating indexing strategies, compression methods, and query processing algorithms.

Technically, the system builds an inverted index over a document corpus, storing per-term document lists that are traversed at query time entirely from main memory. It supports Boolean conjunction and disjunction queries as well as ranked retrieval using term-frequency and document-frequency signals, including TF/IDF-style normalization. Multiple index compression codecs are implemented, including Partitioned Elias-Fano encoding, yielding index sizes in the 10–40 GiB range for corpora of approximately 50 million web documents. Query latency for top-10 retrieval on such collections is reported in the 10–40 millisecond range. The toolchain covers document parsing, index construction, document reordering, and index sharding for collections that exceed single-machine memory constraints. The codebase is open-source under a permissive license. Its primary audience is IR researchers seeking a reproducible, modifiable baseline for studying efficiency-oriented innovations in search systems, though it is also usable as a general-purpose indexing and retrieval engine.

A common challenge in large-scale file organization workflows is the computational cost of performing full cryptographic checksums on terabytes of files to identify potential duplicates. Reading and hashing entire files repeatedly across millions of entries consumes significant I/O and processing time, much of which may be unnecessary if files differ early in their content. This tool addresses that bottleneck by generating an estimated SHA-1 checksum derived from only a small subset of a file's data — specifically a portion of its contents combined with file length metadata — rather than processing the entire file. The underlying rationale is that most ordinary files (photos, videos, documents) store distinguishing metadata near the beginning, making partial reads sufficient to differentiate the majority of non-duplicate pairs. The intended usage pattern is a two-phase deduplication pipeline: first apply the fast partial checksum to filter out clearly distinct files, then apply a full SHA-512 (or equivalent) hash only to the smaller set of files that share the same partial checksum. The tool is implemented in C++ using OpenSSL and the Crypto++ library, and supports an optional flag to incorporate file modification timestamps into the hash. It is explicitly not intended for authoritative file identity verification, as matching checksums do not guarantee identical file content.

This tool addresses the challenge of managing fragmented personal knowledge scattered across files, cloud storage, and informal notes, while maintaining privacy and enabling meaningful connections between ideas. The proposed approach is a desktop-based personal knowledge management system combined with a full-featured Markdown editor, designed to keep all data local and under user control.

Technically, the system organizes content into notebooks and sections stored as plain Markdown files on the local filesystem, preserving interoperability and privacy. It builds a knowledge graph over these documents, enabling automatic cross-linking between related sections and surfacing associations as users read or write. Navigation features include a graph-based knowledge explorer, full-text and regular-expression search, tag-based filtering, and retrieval of similar sections through association detection. The editing environment functions as a multi-document Markdown IDE supporting mathematical notation, diagrams, images, outlines, section refactoring, cloning, scopes, and stencils. Organizational features include an Eisenhower matrix and Kanban-style organizer. Content can be exported to HTML or CSV formats suitable for machine learning workflows, and imported from wiki formats. The application is implemented as a native desktop application available across macOS, Windows, and multiple Linux distributions including packaging for Debian, Fedora, Arch, NixOS, and FreeBSD, with Docker support also provided.

A common challenge in systems programming involves building associative data structures that balance insertion speed, memory efficiency, and concurrent access. This C++ library addresses that need by implementing an in-memory key-value store optimized for string-keyed data. The system supports standard operations — retrieval, insertion, and deletion — accessible both by key lookup and by alphabetical index position, accommodating arbitrary-length alphanumeric strings for both keys and values. Technically, the implementation combines compressed tries with binary search trees: the trie structure enables prefix-compressed storage of string keys, reducing memory overhead, while the binary search tree facilitates ordered traversal and index-based access. Together these structures allow the store to handle tens of millions of entries within practical time bounds on commodity hardware. Thread safety is supported, enabling concurrent reads and writes from multiple threads. The library is distributed as a single C++ source file requiring C++14 or later, designed for straightforward integration by inclusion into a consuming project's build. Identified areas for future development include asynchronous, non-blocking retrieval calls. The combination of compressed trie indexing and BST ordering makes this approach suited for workloads requiring both fast keyed lookup and alphabetically ordered enumeration over large in-memory string datasets.

A Go library addresses the problem of programmatic MIME type and file extension detection without relying on external C bindings or system dependencies. The approach uses magic number inspection — examining the raw byte signatures at the beginning (or, for certain formats, deeper within) a file — to infer its type. Technically, the library implements a hierarchical tree structure for detection logic, exploiting the fact that many file formats are containers for others: for example, once a file is identified as a ZIP archive, the detection process traverses only the relevant subtree to check for nested formats such as office document variants, rather than re-evaluating unrelated format families. This reduces the number of comparisons needed per detection. The library accepts input as a byte slice, an `io.Reader`, or a file path, and returns both MIME type string and file extension. To avoid loading entire files into memory, detection from readers and files is limited to reading only the file header by default, though a configurable byte limit allows deeper inspection for formats that store signatures later in the file. The implementation is goroutine-safe, has no external dependencies, supports extension with custom format detectors, and distinguishes between text and binary content. The library acknowledges that magic-number detection is inherently slower and less authoritative than protocol-level metadata and recommends it only as a fallback.

A common friction point in command-line workflows is typing full directory paths for navigation. This tool addresses that by allowing users to specify only the initial characters of each path segment, which the system then expands into a full matching directory path. For example, a short abbreviation like `/u/l/b` resolves to `/usr/local/bin`, and `/pf/mss/100` resolves to `C:\Program Files\Microsoft SQL Server\100` on Windows. The approach requires users to type only the first character (or a disambiguating prefix) of each directory component, separated by the standard path delimiter. The core binary is implemented as a standalone executable that performs the directory resolution and writes the matched path to standard output. When multiple directories match a given abbreviated pattern, the system applies a selection heuristic to choose the most appropriate result. Because shell `cd` is a built-in command that cannot be replaced by an external binary directly, integration requires wrapping the tool in a shell function (for Bash/macOS) or a batch file (for Windows), which captures the resolved path from standard output and passes it to the native `cd` command. The tool supports both Unix-like systems and Windows, with platform-specific installation packages available for each.

A lightweight reverse proxy tool written in Go addresses the common challenge of adding HTTPS termination to existing web servers and static file hosts without modifying application code. Many developers find configuring TLS certificates and renewal complex, particularly when working in languages or frameworks where HTTPS support is difficult to implement directly.

The tool automates TLS certificate acquisition and renewal by integrating with the Let's Encrypt certificate authority, requiring only that the target domain's DNS records point to the host server. It operates as a standalone binary with no external library dependencies, accepting inbound HTTPS traffic on standard port 443 and forwarding requests to backend services running on non-public ports.

Technically, the system supports three operational modes: simple reverse proxying to a single upstream HTTP/HTTPS server specified via command-line flag; path-based routing to multiple upstream hosts defined in a JSON configuration file mapping local URL paths to remote endpoints; and direct static file serving with optional gzip compression and configurable HTTP cache-control headers. Certificates are cached to a configurable directory to avoid hitting Let's Encrypt rate limits across reboots. The tool exposes flags for HTTP and HTTPS port overrides, socket read/write/idle timeouts, and includes a built-in helper that prints systemd unit file instructions for running the process as a persistent Linux service.

A lightweight Go library addresses the repetitive boilerplate involved in serializing and returning JSON or XML responses from HTTP handlers in web APIs. Rather than manually setting content-type headers, marshaling data structures, and writing response bodies in each handler, the library provides a unified abstraction that consolidates these steps into a single configurable struct and method call.

Technically, the library centers on a `Parser` struct that accepts an `http.ResponseWriter`, a content type string (`"json"` or `"xml"`), and an optional root tag field for XML output. Handlers instantiate this struct and call either a `Parse` method or a `Serialize` method, both accepting a `map[string]interface{}` payload along with an optional HTTP status code. The `Parse` method handles key-value field maps typed as a named alias (`Fields`), while `Serialize` accepts arbitrary interface values, allowing more complex data structures to be encoded directly. For XML responses, the root tag field wraps the output in a named root element. The library is distributed as a standard Go module and integrates directly with the standard library's `net/http` package, requiring no external dependencies or middleware frameworks. The approach reduces handler verbosity by abstracting content negotiation and encoding logic into a reusable, configurable type.

A Go library implementing the SOCKS Protocol Version 5 specification addresses the need for a minimal, protocol-faithful abstraction for building proxy clients and servers in Go. The design philosophy emphasizes simplicity and small surface area, with the API structure mirroring the conceptual layers of the protocol itself rather than hiding them behind high-level abstractions.

Technically, the library provides low-level struct types that map directly to protocol messages: negotiation request/reply pairs, username/password sub-negotiation request/reply pairs, connection request/reply pairs, and UDP datagram structures. Each struct exposes constructor functions for both the initiating side (e.g., client) and the receiving side (e.g., server), using `io.Reader` and `io.Writer` interfaces for serialization and deserialization. This allows developers to compose the full handshake flow manually for custom scenarios.

For common use cases, a higher-level API is also provided. A server type accepts a handler interface with separate callbacks for TCP and UDP traffic, and can be instantiated with address, credentials, and timeout parameters. A client type wraps the full SOCKS5 handshake and returns a standard `net.Conn`, enabling drop-in use with existing Go networking code. The library supports full TCP and UDP transport as well as both IPv4 and IPv6 addressing. It is distributed under the MIT License.

A unified developer tooling manager addresses the fragmentation problem in Kubernetes and cloud-native development workflows, where engineers must consult multiple README files, package managers, and vendor download pages to assemble a working environment. The tool operates across two primary modes: a CLI installer that resolves the correct binary for the host's operating system and CPU architecture (supporting Linux, macOS, Windows, Intel, and ARM variants), and a Kubernetes application installer that wraps Helm charts, static manifests, and custom CLI-based installers behind a consistent flag-driven interface.

For CLI acquisition, the system fetches statically-linked binaries from upstream GitHub releases or vendor-specified URLs, caches them under a configurable local path, and supports pinned version downloads and batch acquisition. For Kubernetes applications, it abstracts Helm values files into named flags while preserving an escape hatch via `--set` overrides, enabling reproducible cluster bootstrapping with tools such as ingress controllers, certificate managers, and databases.

Additional capabilities include a system-package installer for Linux-specific daemons and runtimes (with optional systemd integration), extraction of binaries from OCI container images, Helm chart image verification and version-bumping utilities, and compatibility with CI runners through a GitHub Actions integration. The project is implemented in Go and licensed under MIT.

A Go static analysis tool addresses the difficulty of writing custom linting rules for Go codebases without requiring recompilation or plugin infrastructure. The core problem is that existing approaches to codified style enforcement and bug detection typically demand deep toolchain integration or recompilation cycles whenever rules change.

The proposed approach uses a declarative domain-specific language (DSL) expressed as ordinary Go source files, allowing analysts to define pattern-matching rules that are dynamically loaded at runtime. Rules are distributed and versioned as standard Go modules, enabling sharing across projects and teams.

Technically, the system operates in two phases: it first parses rule files written against a dedicated DSL package, then applies the compiled rule set to target Go packages using the `golang.org/x/tools/go/analysis` framework. Each rule is defined as a function accepting a `Matcher` argument; rules chain `Match(patterns...)`, optional `Where(cond)` filter predicates, and a terminal `Report(message)` or `Suggest(replacement)` call. Pattern matching is handled by an underlying AST structural matching engine that supports metavariables (e.g., `$x`), wildcard sequences, and type-pattern constraints. The `Where` clause enables fine-grained filtering based on expression types, purity, text patterns, and other semantic properties. Quickfix suggestions can be automatically applied via a `-fix` flag. The tool integrates with the broader Go linting ecosystem and can be embedded as a library within other static analysis frameworks.

A command-line tool addresses the niche use case of generating elliptic curve key pairs whose public keys contain user-specified vanity strings. While vanity identifiers are well-established for Bitcoin addresses and similar systems, this tooling extends the concept to standard NIST elliptic curves (P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521) used in general-purpose cryptography.

The approach involves brute-force random key generation with concurrent search across all available CPU cores using goroutines. Each generated key pair is evaluated by encoding the uncompressed public key point — concatenated x and y coordinates per ANSI X9.62 section 4.3.6 — as Base64, then checking whether the resulting string contains the target substring at the beginning, end, or anywhere within it. Cryptographic randomness is sourced from the standard library's secure random number generator by default, with an optional faster but less conservative alternative that seeds from secure entropy and then uses a deterministic hashing algorithm for subsequent bytes.

Key practical constraints are documented: search difficulty scales exponentially (approximately 64x per additional character in Base64 space), case-sensitive matching drastically increases search time, and positional constraints at string boundaries may be mathematically unsatisfiable for certain inputs since most coordinate pairs do not correspond to valid curve points. The tool is implemented in Go and supports case-insensitive matching by default to improve search tractability.

A Go package addresses the limitations of the standard `%v` formatter when inspecting complex runtime data structures during debugging. The built-in formatter provides minimal type context, renders pointers as raw addresses, and critically will stack overflow when encountering recursive or self-referential data structures. The library offers a richer stringification approach that produces both single-line and indented multiline output with substantially more diagnostic information. Technically, the system traverses values via reflection, applying type-specific rendering rules: strings are quoted, pointers are prefixed with `*`, interfaces with `@`, structs enclosed in angle brackets with typed field-value pairs, maps with typed key-value notation, and unsigned integer slices rendered as hexadecimal. Functions, channels, nil values, and invalid reflect states each receive distinct symbolic representations. Recursive and duplicate references are handled through a reference-tracking mechanism: the first occurrence of a repeated value is assigned a numeric identifier prefixed with `~`, and subsequent occurrences are replaced with a `$`-prefixed back-reference, preventing infinite traversal. The library optionally uses the `unsafe` package to expose unexported `reflect.Value` and `reflect.Type` fields for deeper inspection, with a compile-time tag (`-tags safe`) or a runtime flag to disable this behavior. Custom types can implement a describer interface to provide domain-specific representations.

A command-line JSON query processor addresses the complexity of existing tools when performing data transformations beyond simple field selection. The proposed approach uses a Lisp-inspired prefix notation syntax where expressions take the form `(function arg1 arg2)`, enabling deeply nested, composable queries that mirror the hierarchical structure of JSON data.

Technically, the tool is implemented in Go and operates as a pipeline processor reading JSON from standard input. Its core abstraction is a context-aware function composition model: each function evaluates its arguments within a specific JSON context, and the primary navigation primitive (`elem`) progressively narrows that context as queries descend into nested structures. Values placed in function-name position implicitly convert to element accessors, reducing verbosity for common traversal patterns.

The system supports a range of data manipulation primitives: `keys` enumerates object fields or array indices, `range` selects index spans, `array` and `object` construct new JSON structures, `zip` merges arrays, and string functions including `join` and `sprintf` (using Go's standard formatting conventions) handle serialization. A dedicated `error` function emits a stack trace mid-evaluation for debugging. Logical comparison operators (`eq`, `lt`, `gt`) are also provided. An optional interactive mode integrates with fuzzy-finder tooling to display live query results. The tool is distributed as a single installable Go binary.

A common challenge in building REST APIs with Go is the lack of opinionated, full-featured frameworks that enforce clean architecture patterns suitable for medium-to-large enterprise projects. Developers often must assemble disparate libraries for routing, validation, authentication, database access, and other concerns, resulting in inconsistent codebases and significant setup overhead.

This framework addresses that gap by providing an all-in-one, opinionated Go web framework specifically designed for REST API development. Rather than optimizing for minimal footprint or prototype use cases, it targets enterprise-level applications where code reliability, maintainability, and consistent architecture are priorities.

Technically, the framework bundles a comprehensive feature set into a single cohesive package: HTTP routing and controllers, middleware support, request parsing, an advanced multi-rule validation system, business transaction handling, JWT and other authentication mechanisms, database integration via ORM, structured logging, CORS handling, WebSocket support, localization, and dynamic query-parameter-driven filtering and pagination. It also includes DTO conversion and model mapping utilities, file system abstractions, and a testing utilities layer. The framework is built natively in Go and follows structured dependency injection and layered architecture conventions, aiming to let developers concentrate on business logic rather than infrastructure wiring. Despite being opinionated in its conventions, the design remains extensible, allowing customization at most integration points.

A Kubernetes operator addresses the challenge of consistently propagating configuration objects across multiple namespaces within a cluster. The problem arises in multi-tenant environments where administrators need common resources — such as Services, Endpoints, and NetworkPolicy objects — to exist in many namespaces simultaneously, without manually duplicating them or relying on platform-specific mechanisms like OpenShift project templates, which offer limited flexibility.

The approach introduces a custom resource definition called `SyncConfig` that declaratively specifies which Kubernetes objects should be replicated and which namespaces should receive them. Target namespaces are identified through Kubernetes label selectors or explicit name selectors, allowing fine-grained or broad targeting. An optional `prune` parameter ensures that previously synced objects are cleaned up when they are no longer desired, maintaining consistency between the declared configuration and cluster state.

Technically, the system is implemented as a Kubernetes operator using the Operator SDK and written in Go. It watches `SyncConfig` resources and reconciles the desired state across matched namespaces. Object definitions within a `SyncConfig` support parameterized string substitution — for example, injecting the target namespace name dynamically — enabling templated resource generation without external tooling. The operator is distributed as a container image and integrates standard Kubernetes RBAC and controller patterns. Testing infrastructure includes unit tests, integration tests, and end-to-end tests executed via a Bash-based Kubernetes testing framework.

A common challenge in multi-service or multi-container environments is monitoring log output from several concurrent processes simultaneously without switching between terminal windows or running separate monitoring sessions. This tool addresses that problem by providing a unified log aggregation view for multiple commands run in parallel. The approach involves reading a list of shell commands from standard input (one per line) and executing them concurrently, then multiplexing their output streams into a single terminal display with per-command prefixes for visual disambiguation. Each command's output is labeled either by the command string itself or by a user-specified prefix using a `{prefix}: {command}` syntax, allowing operators to assign human-readable identifiers to each stream. A practical use case demonstrated is aggregating log streams from all running Docker containers by combining Docker's process listing capabilities with the tool via standard Unix piping and argument substitution. The implementation is written in Go and distributed as a compiled binary for direct installation. The design relies entirely on standard input for command ingestion, making it composable with existing shell pipelines and scripting workflows without requiring configuration files or persistent daemon processes.

A lightweight serverless functions runtime addresses the operational overhead associated with running container orchestration platforms like Kubernetes for workloads that don't require cluster-scale infrastructure. The approach reimplements a serverless gateway and function execution environment on a single Linux host, targeting resource-constrained environments such as edge deployments, single VMs, or single-board computers with as little as 2 vCPU and 2GB RAM.

Technically, the system is implemented as a single Go binary that runs as a systemd service. Rather than relying on a full container orchestration layer, it uses containerd directly as the container runtime and the Container Networking Interface (CNI) for network provisioning between function containers. This architecture preserves compatibility with the broader serverless ecosystem — the same OCI-compliant function containers, gateway, queue worker, event connectors, and scale-to-zero components used in the Kubernetes-based variant operate unchanged here. Persistent volumes are supported, enabling stateful sidecar services such as databases and monitoring tools to run alongside functions. The system supports x86_64 and ARM64 architectures, making it suitable for Raspberry Pi and similar ARM-based edge hardware. Deployment can be automated via cloud-init, Terraform, or standard shell scripts. The design philosophy prioritizes a stable API surface and minimal ongoing maintenance compared to managing a full Kubernetes cluster.

A common requirement in distributed systems built on the Raft consensus algorithm is a reliable, persistent backend for storing log entries and stable configuration state. Most existing backends rely on embedded key-value stores, but there is interest in using SQLite as an alternative embedded storage engine for this purpose. This library provides a Go package implementing both the LogStore and StableStore interfaces required by a popular Raft consensus library, backed by SQLite as the underlying storage engine. The LogStore interface handles append-only storage and retrieval of Raft log entries, including operations such as appending entries, fetching entries by index, and deleting log ranges during compaction. The StableStore interface manages small amounts of persistent key-value metadata, such as the current term and last voted candidate, which must survive process restarts. Internally, the implementation maps these two interfaces onto SQLite tables, using structured SQL queries for reads and writes. This approach leverages SQLite's ACID transaction guarantees and its widespread availability as a zero-configuration embedded database, providing an alternative to BoltDB-based backends while maintaining full compatibility with the Raft library's storage interface contracts. The package is written in Go and intended as a drop-in backend replacement for distributed applications using the Raft consensus protocol.

A console-based text editor addresses the need for a minimal, understandable implementation of core editor functionality that can serve both practical use and educational purposes. The approach focuses on building a fully functional terminal text editor from scratch using Go and the termbox library, keeping the codebase simple enough to serve as a teaching reference for developers learning how text editors are constructed internally. Technically, the system renders a text editing interface directly in the terminal using termbox for low-level terminal cell manipulation and keyboard input handling. Core features include loading, editing, and saving plain text files; text selection with copy, cut, and paste operations; and incremental text search. All interaction is driven through a keyboard interface, with a built-in shortcut reference accessible via a key combination. The editor is built with a straightforward Makefile-based build system that handles dependency resolution and compilation. Binaries are distributed for Debian/Ubuntu Linux and Windows environments. The project is released under the MIT license, making it freely usable and modifiable. Its primary value proposition is twofold: as a lightweight terminal editor for basic text editing tasks, and as a readable, approachable codebase illustrating the fundamental data structures and rendering logic required to implement an interactive text editor from the ground up.

A Kubernetes operator that addresses the lack of functional LoadBalancer services in non-cloud Kubernetes environments (local clusters, homelabs, on-premises deployments, Raspberry Pi, etc.) where cloud provider integrations are unavailable, leaving services perpetually in a `<pending>` state. The approach automatically provisions public TCP load balancer access by creating a lightweight VM on a supported public cloud provider and establishing a secure tunnel between that VM and the local cluster.

Technically, the operator watches for Kubernetes Services of type `LoadBalancer` and, upon detection, provisions a small VM on a configured cloud provider (supporting AWS EC2, GCE, DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Vultr, Linode, and others) via a shared provisioning library. A tunnel server process runs on the VM, while a corresponding tunnel client runs inside the cluster as a Deployment. Once the TCP tunnel is established, the operator patches the Service resource with the VM's public IP address, replicating the behavior of managed cloud Kubernetes engines. A custom `Tunnel` resource tracks tunnel state and host lifecycle. Services can be selectively managed or excluded via annotations, and proxy protocol (v1/v2) can be enabled to preserve original client IP addresses. Deleting or annotating a Service triggers VM deprovisioning, keeping resource usage in check. The operator runs on both x86_64 and arm64 architectures and integrates with standard ingress controllers and service mesh gateways.

A kubectl plugin addresses the challenge of visualizing and understanding ownership relationships among Kubernetes objects in a cluster. When managing complex deployments, operators often need to trace how high-level resources (such as Deployments or custom resources) decompose into intermediate and leaf objects, but the standard kubectl tooling does not natively render these hierarchies. The tool traverses `ownerReferences` metadata embedded in Kubernetes objects to construct and display a tree of ownership relationships, starting from a specified root resource and recursively discovering all owned descendants across the cluster's API groups. It queries the Kubernetes API dynamically, supporting all resource types including custom resources from third-party controllers (e.g., Knative, Agones). Users can scope queries by namespace, filter resources by label selectors, restrict traversal to specific API groups or resource types using glob patterns (including negation), and control the condition types checked for status reporting. Color-coded output reflects object readiness states. Filtering by API group or resource type can substantially reduce API server load in large clusters, though filtering out intermediate owner types will halt traversal at those points, potentially omitting child resources. The plugin is distributed via the standard Kubernetes plugin manager and is implemented as a standard kubectl plugin following the binary naming convention.

A common challenge in password management is balancing security with accessibility and simplicity. This tool addresses that by providing a terminal-based user interface for managing passwords stored in GPG-encrypted files, built with Go and a text-based UI library.

The approach centers on compatibility with the OpenPGP/GnuPG ecosystem, meaning encrypted password files can be decrypted and read using standard GPG tooling independently of the application itself. Passwords are organized in a plaintext delimited format — service, username, password, and comment fields — making the decrypted output straightforward to search with standard Unix utilities such as grep.

Technically, the system is implemented in Go and uses a terminal UI framework to provide an interactive text interface for browsing and managing password entries. Encryption and decryption rely on the GnuPG/OpenPGP standard, delegating cryptographic operations to established, widely-audited tooling rather than implementing custom encryption. The structured flat-file format prioritizes human readability and interoperability: once decrypted, the file requires no special parser. Installation is handled through the standard Go toolchain. The design philosophy favors minimal dependencies, transparency of the storage format, and compatibility with existing GPG key infrastructure, making it suitable for users who prefer command-line workflows and want to avoid proprietary or opaque password storage formats.

A common challenge in concurrent Go programs is managing large numbers of goroutines efficiently without exhausting system resources or exceeding rate limits. Uncontrolled goroutine spawning can lead to memory pressure and unpredictable behavior, while naive throttling mechanisms add unnecessary complexity. This Go library addresses these concerns by implementing the worker pool pattern, allowing programs to execute a large number of tasks concurrently while bounding the number of simultaneously active goroutines.

The library provides a minimalistic, zero-dependency API for creating goroutine pools that scale dynamically: worker goroutines are created on demand and removed when idle, enabling scale-to-zero behavior. Pools support both bounded and unbounded task queues, blocking and non-blocking task submission, and dynamic pool resizing. Tasks can be submitted in fire-and-forget mode, as awaitable futures returning typed results or errors, or grouped together for collective completion tracking. Task groups support context propagation, enabling cancellation of queued and in-flight work when a context is cancelled or times out. Panics within tasks are captured and surfaced as errors rather than crashing the program. Subpools can be created to share a fraction of a parent pool's concurrency limit. Pool metrics—including running worker count and queue depth—are available for monitoring. The implementation targets high throughput and efficient resource utilization under heavy workloads.

A common need in developer tooling and build systems is locating configuration files or project roots by traversing the filesystem hierarchy upward from a given starting point, rather than relying on absolute paths or environment variables. This Go library addresses that need by implementing a directory-walking search that moves from a specified directory toward the filesystem root until it finds a matching file or directory entry. The library exposes two functions: one that begins the upward traversal from the current working directory, and one that accepts an explicit starting path as a parameter. Both functions accept a target filename or directory name as input and return the path of the first matching entry found among the ancestor directories. The implementation is intentionally minimal, providing a focused utility with no external dependencies beyond the Go standard library. This pattern is common in tools that need to locate files such as configuration manifests, lock files, or project descriptors regardless of the subdirectory from which a command is invoked—mirroring behavior found in similar filesystem traversal utilities in other ecosystems. The library is distributed as a standard Go package and follows conventional Go module conventions for import and installation.

This Go package addresses the challenge of building Progressive Web Applications (PWAs) without requiring JavaScript, enabling Go developers to write both frontend and backend code entirely in a single language. The approach compiles Go code to WebAssembly for client-side execution while leveraging Go's standard HTTP interfaces for server-side routing and request handling. Technically, the library provides a declarative, component-based UI model in which developers construct and compose HTML elements using pure Go syntax — calling chainable builder methods that represent HTML tags, attributes, and event handlers. UI components are defined as Go structs embedding a base compositor type, with a `Render` method returning a tree of UI elements. Conditional rendering and composition are handled through functional helpers within the same Go code. On the server side, the framework integrates directly with the standard `net/http` package: a handler type serves the application shell and static assets, while route registration maps URL paths to component constructors. The compiled WebAssembly binary runs in the browser, enabling the application to operate in its own window, function offline via service worker support, and remain indexable by search engines through server-side rendering compatibility. The package requires Go modules and a recent Go toolchain version.

This framework addresses the challenge of extending container orchestration and device management capabilities to edge computing environments, where network connectivity to centralized cloud infrastructure may be unreliable or intermittent. Rather than building a separate edge management system, the approach extends the existing Kubernetes API surface to cover edge nodes and physical devices, enabling unified management from the cloud using familiar Kubernetes primitives including Custom Resource Definitions.

Technically, the system is split into cloud-side and edge-side components. On the cloud side, a WebSocket server watches for resource changes and relays messages to edge nodes, while two extended Kubernetes controllers manage edge node metadata and device state synchronization respectively. On the edge side, a lightweight agent handles containerized workload lifecycle management, a WebSocket client maintains the cloud connection and synchronizes resource state, and an MQTT client bridges physical IoT devices to the rest of the system via publish/subscribe messaging. A device twin component stores and synchronizes device status locally, and a metadata manager persists Kubernetes resource data to a lightweight SQLite database, enabling edge nodes to operate autonomously when disconnected from the cloud. An HTTP client component additionally allows cloud-initiated communication with REST services running at the edge. The entire edge agent is designed to run on resource-constrained hardware, supporting workloads such as machine learning inference, image recognition, and event processing at the data source.

A React Native library addresses the common limitation that mobile ads are typically rendered inside WebViews, which prevents developers from customizing their appearance to match application design. The proposed approach uses the AdMob Native Advanced ad format, which retrieves raw ad assets — including images, headlines, and video content — directly from ad servers rather than loading a pre-rendered web page. Technically, the library communicates with AdMob servers to receive structured ad data, then passes this information across the React Native bridge, where it is rendered using standard React Native View and Text components. A small number of elements use custom native components where platform constraints require it, but the majority of the ad layout is constructed entirely in JavaScript. This architecture gives developers complete control over ad styling, enabling them to match ad units to application color schemes and typography without managing platform-specific layout files such as XML or XIB. The library supports both iOS and Android with consistent behavior across platforms, and includes features such as configurable auto-refresh intervals, video ad support, ad mediation including third-party network integration, ad targeting, and TypeScript type definitions. The library is implemented as an npm package and is cross-platform.

A common challenge in web development prototyping is that unstyled HTML looks visually rudimentary, yet applying a full CSS framework requires learning class naming conventions and adding markup scaffolding. This stylesheet addresses that gap by providing aesthetic default styling for standard HTML elements without requiring any class names, custom attributes, or framework-specific markup. The approach targets semantic HTML elements directly using CSS element and attribute selectors, meaning a developer can write plain, valid HTML and receive a clean, readable visual presentation automatically. Technically, the stylesheet applies consistent typography, spacing, color schemes, and layout rules to native elements such as headings, paragraphs, forms, buttons, tables, navigation, and sectioning elements. Because styling is applied purely through element selectors rather than utility classes or component abstractions, no JavaScript is involved and there is no build step or configuration required. Integration consists of a single stylesheet link tag referencing a CDN-hosted file, or alternatively installation via a package manager for local bundling. The intended use case is rapid prototyping, minimum viable product development, and situations where a developer wants a presentable result from semantic HTML alone without investing time in design or learning a component library.

A Go library addresses the need for a unified serialization solution that handles struct persistence across multiple storage backends with optional security and compression features. The approach combines binary serialization (pickling/unpickling) of arbitrary Go structs with pluggable storage modes and optional data transformation layers including compression and encryption. Technically, the library serializes Go structs into byte arrays through a pickle operation and deserializes them via the inverse unpickle operation, exposing a consistent read/write/delete interface across four storage backends: in-memory, local filesystem, embedded key-value database (defaulting to LevelDB), and a remote TCP-based RPC server. The database backend is configurable and built on top of an existing Go key-value abstraction layer. The remote TCP mode allows serialized structs to be shared across services by hosting a pickle server that accepts networked read/write/delete requests, enabling distributed access to persisted data. Each storage mode is selected via a mode constant passed to the unified read/write/delete API, making it straightforward to swap persistence strategies without changing application logic. The in-memory mode operates purely on byte slices without any backend. The design targets use cases where Go structs need to be durably stored, transmitted, or shared between services with minimal serialization boilerplate.

This project addresses the whimsical but illustrative problem of exposing FizzBuzz logic as a networked service, offloading modulo arithmetic from client-side computation to a dedicated REST endpoint. The approach wraps the classic FizzBuzz algorithm in a PHP-based HTTP API that returns JSON-formatted responses, supporting both URL query parameters and clean URL path routing via rewrite rules. Two endpoints are provided: one returns the FizzBuzz value for a single integer (responding with a JSON string of "Fizz", "Buzz", "FizzBuzz", or the number itself), and another returns a JSON array of all FizzBuzz values from one up to and including a specified integer. The implementation is packaged as a Docker container for straightforward deployment. An OpenAPI 3.0 specification describes both endpoints formally, enabling integration with standard API tooling. Performance characteristics have been evaluated using a Node.js benchmarking utility, with results documented for large upper-bound requests. The project is licensed under MIT and is intended partly as a demonstration of REST API design and documentation practices — illustrating endpoint definition, path parameterization, and response schema specification — using a universally recognizable algorithmic problem as the underlying domain.

A desktop application addresses the need to read locally stored password vault files (specifically the OPVault format) on Linux without relying on proprietary client software. The proposed approach implements a JavaFX-based graphical interface that parses and decrypts OPVault data entirely on the local machine, following a security-conscious design philosophy. Technically, the tool uses zero-copy/zero-allocation JSON parsing to extract only necessary fields from the OPVault JSON structures, immediately zeroing out in-memory buffers after use. All credential data is stored in encrypted form in memory and decrypted transiently only when needed for copy or auto-fill operations, minimizing the window of exposure for sensitive plaintext. The interface follows a Material Design aesthetic and includes a quick-filter mechanism for locating vault entries. TOTP (time-based one-time passwords) are supported, while HOTP is omitted due to its requirement for write access to the vault. An auto-type feature allows the application to inject credentials (username, password, or both) into the previously focused window. The application is built with Java and JavaFX, requires OpenJDK 11 or later, and is currently targeted at Linux, with macOS and Windows builds under development. The build system uses Gradle, with native installer packaging via jpackage planned.

Reference counting garbage collection in managed languages like Java typically relies on supplemental tracing passes to handle cyclic references, complicating implementations and introducing latency. This project implements a pure reference counting garbage collector in Java, based on the academic algorithm described by Bacon et al., which eliminates the need for a separate cycle-detection tracing phase. The core technical approach centers on a deferred cycle collection mechanism: rather than immediately attempting to reclaim cyclic structures, candidate objects suspected of being part of cycles are buffered and processed in a dedicated collection phase. This phase performs a trial deletion—temporarily decrementing reference counts to identify groups of objects whose counts drop to zero only when internal cycle references are excluded—allowing the collector to safely reclaim cyclic garbage using reference counting alone. The implementation is written in Java and serves as a practical demonstration of the Bacon et al. algorithm in an object-oriented runtime environment. By encoding the required reference count manipulation, purple/gray/black/white object coloring states, and buffered candidate tracking directly in Java, the project provides an executable reference for researchers and implementers studying alternative garbage collection strategies. The work focuses on algorithmic correctness and fidelity to the original paper rather than integration with production JVM internals.

This library addresses a limitation in Spring Data JPA where `EntityGraph` definitions must be statically bound to repository methods via annotations at compile time, preventing runtime selection of fetch strategies based on contextual needs. The approach extends Spring Data JPA's repository infrastructure to accept `EntityGraph` instances as method arguments, enabling dynamic control over JPA entity fetch plans at query execution time.

Technically, the library introduces a custom repository factory bean that replaces the default Spring Data JPA factory, enabling interception of repository method calls to apply a supplied `EntityGraph` to the underlying JPA query. It provides counterpart interfaces for all standard Spring Data JPA repository interfaces (e.g., `CrudRepository`, `JpaRepository`, `QuerydslPredicateExecutor`) that overload each predefined method with an additional `EntityGraph` parameter. Three `EntityGraph` implementation strategies are supported: `NamedEntityGraph` references a pre-registered named graph by string identifier; `DynamicEntityGraph` constructs ad-hoc fetch graphs by specifying attribute paths at runtime; and a type-safe composer generated via a compile-time annotation processor that leverages JPA metamodel information (compatible with tools such as `hibernate-jpamodelgen`) to produce strongly-typed, autocomplete-friendly graph builder classes per entity. Additionally, repositories can declare a default `EntityGraph` that applies when no explicit graph is passed, with explicit arguments always taking precedence.

This project addresses the need for a minimal, dependency-free information-sharing site that can operate in low-infrastructure or emergency environments — including offline scenarios using only a local WiFi router and a computer. The approach is a static, link-aggregator interface modeled loosely on social news sites, where all content is managed by directly editing a plain JSON file rather than through a database or content management system. Technically, the system consists of pre-built static files that require no installation; users unzip the package and either serve it from any static hosting platform or run it locally using a language runtime's built-in HTTP server (such as PHP's single-threaded development server). Content is structured as a JSON array of objects, each containing a title, URL, date, and username field, making it editable with any text editor without specialized tooling. The minimal footprint is intentional, optimizing for slow network connections and constrained environments. The current implementation functions as an MVP focused solely on hyperlink listings, with user authentication, content submission, and commenting described as potential future additions. The design was motivated by real-world infrastructure disruptions, prioritizing resilience and portability over feature completeness.

This JavaScript library addresses the need for a lightweight, human-readable persistence layer for small projects that do not require a full relational or document database engine. Rather than introducing a separate database server or binary storage format, the approach stores all data directly on the local filesystem as plain JSON files, organized into subdirectories.

Technically, each table maps to a directory, each record is stored as an individual JSON file, and table metadata is kept in a separate `tableInfo.json` file. Indexes are supported on top-level object properties, with each indexed property receiving its own nested subdirectory containing one JSON file per unique index value. The API exposes a small surface: configuring a root path, creating or dropping tables, putting and getting records by key, and querying indexed tables by property value to retrieve matching keys or full records. Both standard and indexed table variants are provided, with indexed tables enabling equality lookups via `getAllMatchingKeysFromIndex` and `getAllMatchingRecordsFromIndex`. Auto-generated or custom string keys are supported, and any JSON-serializable value can be stored. Because all data is plain text, the database directory can be placed under version control, making record-level changes human-readable and diffable. The implementation is written in approximately 500 lines of JavaScript with two dependencies, and the roadmap includes cursor-based pagination, transactions, and ACID guarantees for single-threaded access.

A common challenge for researchers, offline workers, and privacy-conscious users is retaining and retrieving web content they have previously browsed, without depending on remote servers or third-party services. This tool addresses that problem by creating a locally stored, fully searchable offline web archive. The approach involves running a local intercepting proxy that integrates directly with the browser's fetch cycle, automatically capturing every page visited during a browsing session. Captured content is indexed for full-text search, enabling users to retrieve previously visited pages without internet connectivity. The system operates in two primary modes: a save mode that archives and indexes content as the user browses, and a serve mode that replays saved content as if the user were still online. The implementation is built on Node.js and can be installed as an npm package, run directly from source, or distributed as a pre-built binary for Windows, macOS, and Linux. A local web-based control panel, accessible via localhost, provides search functionality, configuration options, and archive management. All data remains on the user's local machine, with no external transmission. Advanced configuration allows users to specify archive storage locations, tune Node.js runtime memory parameters for large archives, and blacklist domains from being captured.

This project demonstrates a micro-frontend architecture that integrates React and AngularJS applications within a single web page using a micro-frontend orchestration framework. The core problem addressed is how to compose multiple independently developed frontend applications — built with different JavaScript frameworks — into a cohesive user interface without requiring a full rewrite or tight coupling between codebases. This is particularly relevant for teams migrating legacy AngularJS applications toward modern frameworks incrementally.

The technical approach relies on a single-spa orchestrator, which acts as a top-level router and lifecycle manager. Each sub-application (one built with React, one with AngularJS) is registered as a separate micro-frontend with its own mount, unmount, and bootstrap lifecycle hooks. The orchestrator dynamically activates or deactivates each application based on the current URL route. Specifically, navigating to one route renders only the React application, another route renders only the AngularJS application, and a root route renders both simultaneously within the same browser context. Dependencies are installed via npm or Yarn, and the development server runs on a local port exposing distinct URL paths for each sub-application. This pattern enables framework-agnostic composition, allowing teams to deliver features independently per sub-application while sharing a unified shell and URL-based routing layer.

A self-hosted link aggregation system addresses the need for a personally controlled, curated feed of links drawn from social news and discussion platforms. Rather than relying on third-party aggregators, the approach involves deploying serverless infrastructure that periodically fetches top links from sources such as a well-known tech news forum and configurable subreddits, then renders them as a static webpage. Technically, the system is built with Node.js and deployed to AWS using the Serverless Framework, which provisions a CloudFormation stack managing the underlying resources. Scheduled Lambda functions handle the scraping and link retrieval logic, with results written to an S3 bucket configured for static website hosting.
