A common challenge in modern web development is managing client-side data with reactive, low-latency updates that integrate cleanly across multiple frontend frameworks. This library addresses that gap by providing a client-side, in-memory JavaScript database with a MongoDB-style query interface and full TypeScript support. Rather than relying on server round-trips for immediate UI feedback, it enables optimistic UI patterns by maintaining a local document store that responds instantly to reads and writes. The core abstraction is a schema-less collection supporting familiar query operators (e.g., `$set`, `find`, `updateOne`, `removeOne`) operating on plain JavaScript objects. Reactivity is achieved through a signal-based mechanism: cursors returned by queries automatically re-execute within reactive contexts, meaning UI components that consume query results re-render when underlying data changes without manual subscription management. The system is framework-agnostic, exposing adapters that bridge its internal reactivity model to the signal primitives of Angular, React, Solid, Svelte, and Vue. Persistence is handled through pluggable storage providers, allowing the in-memory store to synchronize with various backends or local storage mechanisms. Data from multiple sources can be aggregated and kept consistent via a synchronization layer. The library is distributed as an npm package written in TypeScript and licensed under MIT.

A common friction point in TypeScript-based projects is the need to repeatedly reimplement utility logic across codebases, often pulling in heavyweight dependencies for small, self-contained functionality. This collection addresses that gap by providing a library of reusable TypeScript snippets designed to be copied directly into projects rather than installed as external packages. The approach is inspired by component-distribution patterns where source code ownership transfers to the consuming project, avoiding dependency version conflicts and reducing bundle bloat. Technically, each snippet is a standalone TypeScript module that can be pasted into any TypeScript project without modification. For developers who prefer automation, an optional command-line interface is provided: running the tool via a package executor allows users to list all available snippets or import a specific snippet into a designated destination directory within their project. The CLI accepts a snippet identifier and a target path as arguments, copying the relevant source file accordingly. No attribution is required, and no persistent installation of the tooling itself is necessary — the CLI is invoked ephemerally. This model keeps the snippets fully auditable and modifiable by the consuming developer, treating the snippets as owned source code rather than opaque third-party dependencies.

A common challenge in frontend development is the manual effort required to translate visual designs — including sketches, wireframes, and design tool exports — into functional HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. This open-source tool addresses that gap by accepting a design image as input and automatically generating corresponding web code. The approach leverages a multimodal large language model (GPT-4 Vision) to interpret the visual structure, layout, and styling of uploaded design screenshots and produce clean, responsive frontend code. Technically, the system is built on a Next.js framework, with an API route that handles image submission and communicates with the vision-capable language model to perform the image-to-code translation. The user uploads a design image — sourced from tools such as Figma, Adobe XD, hand-drawn wireframes, or any screenshot — and the backend processes the image through the vision model, which interprets UI components, typography, spacing, and color, then outputs structured HTML/CSS/JS. The resulting code is returned to the user for direct use or further refinement. The tool is deployable as a self-hosted instance via standard serverless infrastructure, making it accessible for individual developers or teams seeking to accelerate the design-to-implementation workflow without manual transcription of visual specifications.

A command-line tool addresses the problem of visual ambiguity in user interfaces where multiple actions share the same base icon — for example, distinguishing "save project" from "save audio" when both conceptually map to a save icon. The proposed approach draws inspiration from composite icons in the Material Icons library (such as the "edit note" icon, which combines two distinct glyphs into a single unified symbol) and automates that combination process programmatically.

Technically, the tool accepts a YAML recipe file that maps output filenames to pairs of Material Icons specified by name, joined with a `+` operator. It then processes these pairs and merges the corresponding SVG assets, positioning one icon as the primary glyph and overlaying a smaller secondary glyph in the corner to create a compound icon. The system supports both standalone SVG files and SVG files containing multiple `<symbol>` elements, making it compatible with icon sprite workflows. Output files are written to a specified directory. The tool is distributed as an npm package and invoked via a CLI command, taking the recipe file and output path as arguments. This enables design-system maintainers and front-end developers to programmatically generate semantically distinct icon variants without manually editing SVG markup for each combination.
